I live about 2 hours east of Chicago. Northern Indiana/Southern Michigan. Weather varies. Some days you get 60 degrees in January. The next you might have -10 with 3 feet of snow. Summer time can either be really humid or really dry. As for the people. We're nice and homely, but don't expect to have an intelligent conversation with anyone. Those who do have a college degree tend to be the liberal retards. Those without one only know a certain degree of topics. Cars, farm animals, sports. That's about it. Now heres the catchy part. Within a 45 minute drive you have varying degrees of towns/cities. West to east.

There is the first that's relatively a city. The only reason it's on the map is because it borders Lake Michigan and all the rich Chicago people with million dollar beach houses live there during the summer. That's the only time to live in that city. It's also the only reason there are any name brand stores there. And even then they are only outlet stores.

The next is trying to be this "up and coming" city. Still has that home town feel, but developing and gaining new corporate businesses. But the people there aren't the best. The small business owners like to over charge and give really shitty service.

The next town, well idk if you can even call it a town. If you blink you miss it. They have a gas station, a restaurant and a post office. But there you'll find the polite, smile and help you out with anything type of people. It's only minutes from the previously mentioned town so not too much of a trouble doing errands. Unless you want to find a big corporate store. The nearest Starbuck is 30 minutes in either direction. So it's obviously rural, but not have no cell service/internet rural.

Edit: I forgot a town here. * This town is small. But not as small as the last. This one has a fire department, post office, small locally owned furniture store and grocery store. A small park. Library and several other locally owned businesses. It's a tight knit community where everyone knows everyone and their business. There are several great restaurants. An Irish Pub/restaurant. A very authentic German/Austrian restaurant where the owner actual was born and lived in Austria. His family still visits every year. A typical mexican restaurant. A pizza/bowling place. You get the idea. Now the downside to this town is that it's run my a bunch of old ladies. They want to preserve the historical aspect of the town. They don't allow any outside corporate businesses in other than gas stations, a Dollar General and a CVS (for their meds of course). They have the room and potential to grow this city, but won't. Because of that taxes are high. A lot of the businesses end up closing after a year or two because there just isn't the business they need to pay the high property rent. Same goes for housing. There is one small apartment complex, but it's always filled up because the area is close to an elementary school and high school. So a lot of families who can't afford the high taxes live there. There aren't many rentable houses either. If there are any they all have occupants who have been living there for years. The same train station mentioned below runs through this town as well as the first city to Chicago. From this station it's about a 2 hour ride. It's definitely a nice place to visit or go on a date, but as far as living not so much.

The last actual city is actually more like 2 cities combined. South Bend/Mishawaka. Now I know someone on here mentioned don't do college towns. And if this was something like Laffayette, IN with Purdue I'd agree. Between South Bend/Mishawaka you have i believe it's 5 colleges. All except one are religious colleges. Now I say these cities are combined because you could be on one street with a South Bend address, but the next street is a Mishawaka address. It's very weird and confusing and some of the long time residents don't quite understand it. Because of the two cities being so close together you get almost double the corporate businesses. You'll have two Targets, two Kohl's, two of almost whatever store within 10 minutes of each other. Kinda nice if one store doesn't have what you want/need. We have a mall that's decent. It does include an Apple store. Idk why the chose this area, but it's there. There is a train station that you can use to get to Chicago if you absolutely want/need. Many people will take a weekend trip up there or go visit a museum for a day then come home. It's about a 2-3 hour ride though. There are many local shops and a nice farmers market. We do run low on some resources though. Like for internet we have the choices of AT&T or Comcast. The people vary, but most are nice, helpful and polite. Unless you get that one wanna be ghetto white kid. The old people always tend to be very bitter though. Mishawaka has a beautiful Central Park and river walk. Their parks and rec department could use some help. Not many adult sports activities, but they have some very beautiful parks. Speaking of parks there are about 5 county parks that are just beautiful to hike, bike, kayak, canoe in. If you were to drive another 45 minutes east you'd run into Amish country.

And that's Northern Indiana for you. Like the first commenter pointed out. It all depends on what your career is. Northern IN offers a lot of blue collar jobs. Not much for white collar jobs. If you want to attend any concerts you'll be driving at least 2 hours to the nearest venue. Obviously these towns aren't towns where you can just walk wherever. The first and last cities do have local transportation. But all it is, is a bus service. Taxi service if called upon, very few Ubers, and no subways. So there is definitely a need for you're own car. There also isn't much of a night life except on the weekends. If you're going to the bars during the week you'll find only the alcoholics or single people with nothing better to do.

Anyways I hope this helps. My favorite city to ever visit was San Diego in California. Beautiful weather! Lots to do, but that's all I can offer on that. My boyfriend lived in Savannah, Georgia for about a year. He really enjoyed it, just not the weather. It apparently rained a lot. He also didn't like how high taxes were there. But he came from a very rural part of Indiana where taxes were practically nonexistent. We've both agreed that Tennessee is our favorite state and some day would like to move there. I've always enjoyed the weather and I've never met a mean person.

Good luck!
